## Customize markers based on post data

You may want to set custom markers only for specific posts, based on the post ID, known post data, or the marker’s position. Or you may want to use post data within the custom marker itself.

This can be done both [with the facetwp_map_marker_args PHP hook](#customize-markers-based-on-post-data-with-the-facetwp_map_marker_args-php-hook) and [with the facetwp_map/marker/content JS hook](#customize-markers-based-on-post-data-with-the-facetwp_map-marker-content-js-hook).

Using 
```
facetwp_map_marker_args
```

 is the easiest, because with PHP you can get any post data you need (e.g. categories, terms, or custom fields) using the post ID, which is available in the hook.

When using the 
```
facetwp_map/marker/content
```

 JS hook, the post ID and marker position are also directly available. But when you need to use post data in this hook, you first need to [pass it from the PHP hook to the JS hook in its arguments](#use-custom-post-data-in-the-facetwp_map-marker-content-js-hook).

Within the

### Set a marker altitude

On [vector maps](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map/#choose-a-map-rendering-type), you can set the altitude at which a marker appears. This is useful for making markers appear correctly in relation to 3D map content, when the user uses map tilt ([if the vector map supports that](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map/#map-tilt-and-rotation)).

To set the altitude for a marker, specify an 
```
altitude
```

 property in the 
```
position
```

 argument:

```
How to use custom PHP code?PHP code can be added to your (child) theme's functions.php file. Alternatively, you can use the Custom Hooks add-on, or a code snippets plugin. More info// https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/advanced-markers/collision-behavior#set_marker_altitude
add_filter( 'facetwp_map_marker_args', function( $args, $post_id ) {

  $args['position']['altitude'] = 20; // altitude in meters

return $args;
}, 10, 2 );
```

### Make markers draggable

![A draggable marker.](https://facetwp.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/draggable-marker.png)A draggable marker.
When draggability is enabled, users can drag markers on the map using the mouse or the arrow keys. To make a marker draggable, set the 
```
gmpDraggable
```

 property to 
```
true
```

:

```
How to use custom PHP code?PHP code can be added to your (child) theme's functions.php file. Alternatively, you can use the Custom Hooks add-on, or a code snippets plugin. More info// https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/advanced-markers/draggable-markers
add_filter( 'facetwp_map_marker_args', function( $args, $post_id ) {

  $args['gmpDraggable'] = true;

return $args;
}, 10, 2 );
```

Note that the Legacy Marker’s [draggable property](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/reference/marker#MarkerOptions.draggable) is backward compatible and can still be used.

Note:Markers cannot be draggable if they have an [altitude set](#set-a-marker-altitude). This will result in a Console error.

## Customize the Proximity facet marker pin

![The default yellow Proximity facet marker pin.](https://facetwp.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/proximity-marker-pin-default.png)The default yellow Proximity facet marker pin.
If you are using the map with a [Proximity facet](/help-center/facets/facet-types/proximity/), when a location is entered, a yellow location marker is displayed on the map, as shown in the image on the right.

Like all other markers on the map, the proximity pin is an [Advanced Marker](#introducing-advanced-markers). This means you can customize it in exactly the same way as other markers. You can [customize it as marker pin](#customize-the-marker-pin), or change it into an [HTML marker](#create-an-html-marker).

Below are some simple examples, but you can use any of the customizations described above for normal markers.

The only difference with normal markers, is that when customizing the marker with PHP, you need to use a different hook: 
```
facetwp_map_proximity_marker_args

. This hook works in the same way as 
```

 for normal markers.

### Disable the Proximity facet marker pin

If you want to completely disable the Proximity marker pin, you can use this hook:

```
How to use custom PHP code?PHP code can be added to your (child) theme's functions.php file. Alternatively, you can use the Custom Hooks add-on, or a code snippets plugin. More infoadd_filter( 'facetwp_map_proximity_marker_args', '__return_false' );
```

Be aware that using the above code may lead to unexpected map behavior for users if a Proximity search is performed that has no results (markers). Without any markers (also not the Proximity marker), the map cannot use 
```
fitBounds()
```

, which it normally uses to zoom and pan the map’s viewport to contain the available markers.

If you have enabled [marker clustering](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map/advanced-map-customizations/customize-marker-clustering/), you can also [exclude the Proximity marker pin from the clustering behavior](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map/advanced-map-customizations/customize-marker-clustering/#exclude-the-proximity-marker-pin-from-marker-clustering).

### Example 4: Change the marker icon when an info window is open

![Change marker when info window is open.](https://facetwp.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/marker-change-on-click.gif)Change the marker icon when an info window is open.
The following code example changes the marker icon when an info window is opened, and switches it back when it is closed. This can be useful to indicate an ‘active’ marker with a different design or color.

The code works both when using customized marker icons ([marker pins](#customize-the-marker-pin) or [HTML markers](#create-an-html-marker)) and default marker icons.

First, in [lines 7-21](#change-marker-infowindow-click-L7-L21) we define the ‘active’ marker icon. You can do this [by creating a custom marker pin](#customize-the-marker-pin), or [by using marker HTML](#create-an-html-marker).

In case you are using customized markers icons (marker pins HTML markers) for the unclicked markers, these are stored in [lines 23-29](#change-marker-infowindow-click-L23-L29), so they can be re-set when the info window is closed, another marker is clicked, or when the user clicks anywhere on the map.

In [line 31](#change-marker-infowindow-click-L31) we use the

```

```
post_id

window.marker_post_id

 as the active open marker, and set that marker’s icon to the ‘active’ version, by setting the marker’s direct child element value to the ‘active’ pin or HTML, in [lines 42-44](#change-marker-infowindow-click-L42-L44)

In [line 49](#change-marker-infowindow-click-L49) we use the Google Maps JavaScript API’s [closeclick event](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/reference/info-window#InfoWindow.closeclick) to detect the closing of the info window. When that happens, or when the map is clicked anywhere (causing all info windows to close), or when another marker is clicked, we use FacetWP’s 
```
get_post_markers
```

 function and pass it the stored active marker’s 
```
post_id
```

 so we can switch its icon back to the original one.

### Example 5: Display a circle or other shape around (clicked) markers

![Display a circle or other shape around clicked markers.](https://facetwp.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/marker-click-circle.png)Display a circle (or other shape) around clicked markers.
The following code uses the 
```
facetwp_map/marker/click
```

 hook to draw a circle around a marker when it is clicked. Note that instead of a circle, this could be any other [type of shape/polygon supported by the Google Maps API](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/shapes).

You can customize the circle’s fill color and opacity, and its stroke color, opacity and weight. The circle’s size is determined by the 
```
radius
```

 value (in meters) set in [line 22](#marker-circle-clicked-L22).

Clicking another marker will clear the previous circle. The code (optionally) also removes the circle when any marker’s info window is closed, and/or when you click anywhere on the map.

If you want to apply the code only to certain markers, you can use the clicked marker’s 
```
post_id
```

 to write a condition.

### Example 6: Fade in markers on map load and refresh

The following snippet uses FacetWP’s 
```
facetwp_map/marker/added
```

 hook to let markers fade in when the map loads, and on each refresh (after filtering).

When a marker is added, the 
```
opacity
```

 is set to 
```
0
```

 (invisible). Then, when the 
```
interactionObserver
```

 sees that a marker entering the viewport, it sets the 
```
opacity
```

 to 
```
1
```

, with a 
```
transition
```

 to let the marker fade in over 
```
2.5
```

 seconds, as set in [line 7](#markers-fade-in-L7).

```
How to use custom PHP code?PHP code can be added to your (child) theme's functions.php file. Alternatively, you can use the Custom Hooks add-on, or a code snippets plugin. More infoadd_action('facetwp_scripts', function () {
  ?>
  <script>
    const intersectionObserver = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
      for (const entry of entries) {
        if (entry.isIntersecting) {
          entry.target.style.transition = "all 2.5s"; // Fade in over 2.5 seconds
          entry.target.style.opacity = "1";
          intersectionObserver.unobserve(entry.target);
        }
      }
    });

### Example 7: Animate markers: drop markers on map load and refresh

![Animate markers: drop markers on map load and refresh.](https://facetwp.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/marker-drop-animation.gif)Animate markers: drop markers on map load and refresh ([live demo](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/advanced-markers/html-markers#animated_markers)).
The following snippet uses FacetWP’s 
```
facetwp_map/marker/added
```

 hook to let markers vertically “drop into” the viewport when the map loads, and on each refresh (after filtering).

The 
```
interactionObserver
```

 sees when a marker enters the viewport, and adds the 
```
drop
```

 class, which has a CSS animation attached that animates the vertical (Y) position and 
```
opacity
```

. When the attached 
```
animationend
```

 event listener sees that the animation is ended, it removes the class and sets the 
```
opacity
```

 to 
```
1
```

. Each marker animation starts with a randomized delay, based on a delay value that can be customized in [line 20](#markers-drop-in-L20).

### Example 8: Control marker visibility by map zoom level

The following snippet shows how to control marker visibility by map zoom level.

In this example, markers with post IDs within the 
```
trackedPostIds
```

 array in [line 9](#marker-visibility-by-zoom-level-L9) are hidden when the zoom level is higher than 
```
10
```

 (as set in the 
```
zoomThreshold
```

 variable in [line 12](#marker-visibility-by-zoom-level-L12)).

The code uses an event listener in [line 14](#marker-visibility-by-zoom-level-L14) to listen for the 
```
zoom_changed
```

 [map event](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/events). When it fires, and the zoom level is higher than 
```
zoomThreshold
```

, it uses the 
```
FWP_MAP.markersArray
```

 to filter the array by the 
```
trackedPostIds
```

, and hides each marker that is within it. Markers are hidden by setting their CSS 
```
display
```

 property to 
```
none
```

 in [line 23](#marker-visibility-by-zoom-level-L22).

Note that the zoom level is a value between 
```
1
```

 and 
```
20
```

## What is marker clustering?

![Marker clusters on a map, with default cluster icons.](https://facetwp.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/marker-clustering-default-icons.jpg)Marker clusters on a map, with default cluster icons.
If you have large numbers of markers concentrated in specific regions, marker clustering can help simplify their display by grouping them into clusters.

Clusters will have a cluster icon of which the color and text (or the whole [icon design](#customize-the-marker-cluster-icons)) is based on the total number of markers contained in them.

Each cluster icon on the map will show the number of clustered markers in it. Clusters will “de-cluster” into their contained regular markers at [specified zoom levels](#set-the-maximum-zoom-level-for-a-cluster-to-appear), and/or after  [clicking the cluster](#set-marker-cluster-to-not-zoom-in-when-clicking-on-it).

Marker clustering can be enabled with the [“Marker clustering” setting](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map#enable-marker-clustering) in your Map facet.

with the [“Marker clustering” setting](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map#enable-marker-clustering) in your Map facet.

FacetWP uses the [official Google Maps JavaScript MarkerClusterer library](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/marker-clustering). Its documentation, options, methods and examples can be found [here](https://googlemaps.github.io/js-markerclusterer/). Its GitHub repo can be found [here](https://github.com/googlemaps/js-markerclusterer).

Note that the Map facet has *another* built-in feature that helps deal with markers that are very close together or overlap because they share (almost) the same latitude/longitude: [Overlapping Marker Spiderfier](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map/advanced-map-customizations/customize-overlapping-marker-spiderfier/). Overlapping Marker Spiderfier plays nice with marker clustering: once you get down to a zoom level where clusters de-cluster into individual markers, these markers will then “spiderfy” (fan out) if they are (almost) in the same location.

## Customize clustering options

Since v2.0 of the [Map facet](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map/), there is a new JavaScript hook with which you can set marker clustering options: 
```
facetwp_map/clusterer
```

. This hook filters the [MarkerClustererOptions](https://googlemaps.github.io/js-markerclusterer/interfaces/MarkerClustererOptions.html).

Below are a few clustering options you can customize:

## Customize the marker cluster icons

Just like normal markers, cluster icons are [Advanced Markers](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map/advanced-map-customizations/customize-advanced-markers/#introducing-advanced-markers). Advanced Markers can have two forms: [customizable marker pins](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map/advanced-map-customizations/customize-advanced-markers/#customize-the-marker-pin), or [custom HTML](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map/advanced-map-customizations/customize-advanced-markers/#create-an-html-marker).

There are basically two ways to customize marker cluster icons. The newest and most flexible way is to [use a so-called custom “renderer”](#customize-the-marker-cluster-icons-with-a-custom-renderer) to create and set a custom Advanced Marker for the cluster icon. The advantage of doing it this way is that Advanced Markers are highly customizable, both as marker pin and as HTML marker. Specifically HTML markers can have any form or shape you can dream up. See the [Customize Advanced Markers page](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map/advanced-map-customizations/customize-advanced-markers/#introducing-advanced-markers) for inspiration.

s/facet-types/map/advanced-map-customizations/customize-advanced-markers/#introducing-advanced-markers) for inspiration.

The second way is to use one of the “legacy” cluster configuration options, [as explained below](#legacy-ways-of-customizing-the-marker-cluster-icons). This is way less complex than a custom renderer, and the recommended option for simple cluster icon customizations. Note that under the hood, also these legacy options are converted to Advanced Markers (HTML markers) in a custom renderer.

heading_path: Customize the marker cluster icons with a custom renderer

### Customize the marker cluster icons with a custom renderer

The [Google Maps JavaScript MarkerClusterer library](https://googlemaps.github.io/js-markerclusterer/index.html) that FacetWP uses, makes it possible to customize marker cluster icons by creating and setting a so-called [renderer function](https://googlemaps.github.io/js-markerclusterer/interfaces/Renderer.html) that generates the marker cluster icons.

![Marker cluster icons using DefaultRenderer().](https://facetwp.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/cluster-icons-default-renderer.jpg)Marker cluster icons using DefaultRenderer().
If you don’t use a custom renderer, the [DefaultRenderer() function](https://googlemaps.github.io/js-markerclusterer/classes/DefaultRenderer.html) is used. The 
```
DefaultRenderer
```

 renders marker clusters as a round SVG icon in two colors: blue for small clusters and red for large ones, as shown in the image on the right. A live demo of 
```
DefaultRenderer()
```

 can be seen in the [top left of the library’s cluster demo page](https://googlemaps.github.io/js-markerclusterer/public/renderers/).

### Legacy ways of customizing the marker cluster icons

With “legacy” we mean the situation **before** FacetWP v4.4 with the Map add-on v2.0.

These legacy methods all use the 
```
facetwp_map_init_args

## Customize marker cluster icons by location or post ID

The following elaborate example shows how to customize marker cluster icons based on the location (latitude and/or longitude) of the cluster, or the post IDs of the posts it contains.

In [Part 1](#cluster-icons-based-on-post-data-L9-L115) we define a custom cluster renderer function that determines how the cluster icon is rendered. Then, in [Part 2](#cluster-icons-based-on-post-data-L117-L124), we pass this function into the [renderer](https://googlemaps.github.io/js-markerclusterer/interfaces/Renderer.html) cluster argument.

In [lines 79-112](#cluster-icons-based-on-post-data-L79-L112) we define a custom cluster icon, using a [custom Advanced Marker](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map/advanced-map-customizations/customize-advanced-markers/). In this case, we create an [HTML marker](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map/advanced-map-customizations/customize-advanced-markers/#create-an-html-marker-with-the-facetwp_map-marker-content-js-hook) that consists of an inline SVG icon. We chose the default cluster icon SVG that is already used by the marker clusterer library.

heading_path: What is a marker info window?
text:
## What is a marker info window?

![A marker info window with header content and 'regular' content.](https://facetwp.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/marker-info-window.png)A marker info window with header content and “regular” content.
A marker info window is a standard feature that comes with the Google Maps API. It is basically an overlay that looks like a rounded speech bubble. Its content consists of text/HTML that is related to the marker’s post, and a close (‘X’) icon in the top right. The text/HTML content can be entirely customized, [as explained below](#add-or-customize-marker-info-window-content).

By default, each [Advanced Marker](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map/advanced-map-customizations/customize-advanced-markers/) will have an info window that automatically pops up directly above it when you click the marker. If you don’t want or need info windows, this can be prevented [by making the marker(s) unclickable](#disable-marker-info-windows).

heading_path: What is a marker info window?
text:
’t want or need info windows, this can be prevented [by making the marker(s) unclickable](#disable-marker-info-windows).

Info windows will automatically adapt their size to the amount of content they contain. The size can be customized by setting certain [info window options](#customize-marker-info-window-options), or [with CSS](#change-the-marker-info-window-width-or-height-with-css). The map itself will automatically pan to make room for an opening info window, on click of a marker. So if you click a marker that is near the left edge of the map, the map will pan to the right when clicking the marker, making sure the info window is fully visible, while remaining centered above the clicked marker.

To close an info window, click its close icon. Info windows will also close automatically if you click another marker, or the map itself. By default, only one info window will be open at a time.

The Google Maps API’s [InfoWindow class](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/reference/info-window) has a range of [options](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/reference/info-window#InfoWindowOptions), [methods](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/reference/info-window#InfoWindow-Methods) and [events](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/reference/info-window#InfoWindow-Events) that can be used to influence how the info windows look and behave.

Some of the info window options, like the minimum and maximum width, can be set/customized [using the facetwp_map_marker_args hook](#customize-marker-info-window-options). To a certain extent, you can also [style the info windows themselves](#change-the-marker-info-window-width-or-height-with-css) and [their content](#style-marker-info-window-content-added-with-the-info-window-content-setting) with CSS.

heading_path: What is a marker info window?

ht-with-css) and [their content](#style-marker-info-window-content-added-with-the-info-window-content-setting) with CSS.

Info windows have two types of content. To the left of the close (“X”) icon is the info window **header content**. And below it is its **“regular” content**. If there is no header content, the space to the left of the close icon will remain empty: the regular content will always appear below the close icon. You can [add and customize both the info window header content and the regular content](#add-or-customize-marker-info-window-content).

The “regular” marker info window content can be added [with the Map facet’s “Info window content” setting](#add-or-customize-marker-info-window-content-with-the-info-window-content-setting), or – for more flexibility – [with a hook](#customize-or-overwrite-the-marker-info-window-content-with-a-hook).

## Disable marker info windows

By default, all markers have an info window that opens when the marker is clicked, including the [Proximity marker](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map/advanced-map-customizations/customize-advanced-markers/#customize-the-proximity-facet-marker-pin).

It’s also possible to check if a marker’s info window content is empty, and [if so, make the marker unclickable](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map/advanced-map-customizations/customize-advanced-markers/#make-markers-with-empty-info-window-content-unclickable).

## What is Overlapping Marker Spiderfier?

![Overlapping marker with (almost) the same location will fan-out ('spiderfy') in a circle or spiral on click.](https://facetwp.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/mapfacet-overlapping-marker-spiderfier.png)Overlapping marker with (almost) the same location will fan-out (“spiderfy”) in a circle or spiral on click.
The Map facet has a feature that helps deal with markers that are very close together or overlap because they share (almost) the same latitude/longitude.

The built-in “[Overlapping Marker Spiderfier JavaScript libary](https://github.com/jawj/OverlappingMarkerSpiderfier)” makes markers fan-out (“spiderfy”) into a circle with spokes, on click. Larger numbers ([by default more than 8](#map-init-args-spiderfier-L15)) will fan out into a more space-efficient spiral.

Overlapping Marker Spiderfier plays nice with [marker clustering](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map#enable-marker-clustering): once you get down to a zoom level where clusters de-cluster into individual markers, these markers will then spiderfy if they are (almost) in the same location.

clusters de-cluster into individual markers, these markers will then spiderfy if they are (almost) in the same location.

If you don’t see close markers spiderfy, you may need to adapt the [maxZoom parameter on the marker clusterer](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map/advanced-map-customizations/customize-marker-clustering/#set-the-maximum-zoom-level-for-a-cluster-to-appear), to ensure that it doesn’t cluster close markers all the way to the level that spiderfying would be more helpful behavior.

There is no setting for Overlapping Marker Spiderfier, it is always enabled, and cannot be disabled.

The Overlapping Marker Spiderfier library that FacetWP uses, has several useful [options](https://github.com/jawj/OverlappingMarkerSpiderfier#construction) that determine how the ‘spider parts’ look and behave.

For example, setting the 
```
keepSpiderfied
```

 [option](#map-init-args-spiderfier-L6) to 
```
false
```

And the 
```
circleSpiralSwitchover
```

 [option](#map-init-args-spiderfier-L15) sets the number of markers at which the marker configuration turns into a spiral instead of a circle.

## Overview

![Facet type Number Range](https://facetwp.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/number-range-facet.png)The Number Range facet type allows users to filter content based on a numerical field value.

## Available options

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Data source | Where the value lives (taxonomy, custom field, post attribute). If you also set an “Other data source”, this value will be used for the Min limit. The facet expects a numeric field. |
| Other data source | Use this setting if you want to use a separate value for the Max limit. The facet expects a numeric field. |
| Compare type | This setting is only relevant when the Other data source setting is in use. It determines how the range of the post’s two data source values is compared to the user-selected range. Note that for all compare types, <= and >= comparisons are used:

Basic – the post’s range is inside the user-selected range:

Enclose – the post’s range surrounds the user-selected range:

Intersect – the post’s range intersects at least partially with the the user-selected range: |
| Fields to show | “Min + Max”, “Exact”, “Min”, or “Max”.
If you use two data sources, it is recommended to set this setting to “Min + Max”. If you choose “Min” or “Max”, only that value is compared. If you choose “Exact”, the comparison will use that value for both the upper and the lower limit of the user range. |

d. If you choose “Exact”, the comparison will use that value for both the upper and the lower limit of the user range. |

Note: FacetWP expects a raw, **unformatted** number (and automatically converts the value if needed).

heading_path: Value storage and empty post range values
text:
## Value storage and empty post range values

If a Number Range facet uses two data sources, the lower value is stored as 
```
facet_value
```

, and the upper value is stored as 
```
facet_display_value
```

 in the [index table](/help-center/indexing/).

There are a few things to keep in mind in this situation:

- If a post has no value set for the **first** (main) data source field, the post will **not be indexed**, so it will never appear in the results. The same is true for posts that do not yet have this field set in the database because they have not been saved after adding the custom field in (for example) [Advanced Custom Fields](/help-center/using-facetwp-with/advanced-custom-fields/).
- If a post has no value set for the **second** data source field, or if that field has not yet been saved for the first time, the post will be indexed but the value for the post’s range upper limit will then be set to 
```
0
```

. This may lead to unexpected or illogical results, depending on the “[Compare type](#compare-type)” you have set for the facet.

To prevent the above situations, make sure that if you use two data source fields, all posts actually have two values set.

## Empty Min or Max fields

What happens if a Number Range facet uses two data sources, and a user does not enter a value into the “Min” or “Max” field? It depends on the “[Compare type](#compare-type)” you have set:

- If the facet’s “Compare type” is set to “Basic”, only the field which has a value entered is used in the comparison.
- If the facet’s “Compare type” is set to “Enclose” or “Intersect”, an empty “Min” field will be compared as 
```
-999999999999
```

 and an empty “Max” field as 
```
999999999999
```

. Note that in this case, setting “Enclose” as “Compare type” will lead to 0 results, as the post’s range will never surround these user range values.

## Customize the “Go” button HTML

If you want to change the “Go” input button HTML, you can use the [facetwp_facet_html hook](/help-center/developers/hooks/output-hooks/facetwp_facet_html/) to customize the output HTML string.

Add the following snippet to your (child) theme’s functions.php to change the button HTML from an 
```
<input>
```

 element to a 
```
<button>
```

 element. The 
```
<button>
```

 is added with a 
```
__()
```

 [translatable button text](#translate-the-go-button):

```
How to use custom PHP code?PHP code can be added to your (child) theme's functions.php file. Alternatively, you can use the Custom Hooks add-on, or a code snippets plugin. More infoadd_filter( 'facetwp_facet_html', function( $output, $params  ) {
  if ( 'number_range' == $params['facet']['type'] ) {
    $output = str_replace('<input type="button" class="facetwp-submit" value="Go" />', '<button class="facetwp-submit">' . __( 'Go', 'fwp-front' ) . '</button>', $output);
  }
  return $output;
}, 10, 2 );
```

## Overview

![](https://facetwp.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/facet-type-pager.png)The Pager facet type can be used to add several types of pagination.

It might seem a bit counter-intuitive that pagination can be added as a facet type, but just like any other facet type, a Pager facet can be added by making a new facet in the FacetWP admin interface.

Go to the Facets tab, click “add new”, choose “Pager” as Facet type, choose a [pager type](#choose-a-pager-type), set its [options](#available-options), and place it on your page [with a shortcode](https://facetwp.com/help-center/facets/#displaying-a-facet).

### Choose a pager type

A Pager facet can be used to display **four different pager types**. For each Pager facet you add, you have to choose one of these four pager types in the Pager facet’s options:

1. [Page numbers](#page-numbers-pager-type) (and “Prev” / “Next” links)
2. [Result counts](#result-counts-pager-type)
3. [A “Load more” button](#load-more-pager-type)
4. [A “Per page” box](#per-page-pager-type)

heading_path: Display multiple pager types on a page
text:
### Display multiple pager types on a page

For each pager type you want to display on a page, you need to add **a separate Pager facet** in the FacetWP admin interface, with the “Pager type” option set to its own type. So if you want to display Page numbers *and* Result counts *and* a Per page box, you need to make 3 separate Pager facets and place 3 different [shortcodes](/help-center/developers/shortcodes-reference/#display-a-facet) on the page.

Warning: Don’t use a “Page numbers” and a “Load more” pager type together on one page, these do different things and will not work well together.

heading_path: Display a pager type more than once on page
text:
### Display a pager type more than once on page

If you want to display page numbers (or any of the other pager types) twice (or more) on the same page, for example above and below your post listing, you can just re-use the shortcode for that Pager facet and place it on the page twice.
## Available options

### Pager type

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Pager type | Determines the pager type: Page numbers (and “Prev” / “Next” links), Result counts, a “Load more” button or a “Per page” box |

### “Page numbers” pager type

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Inner size | The number of pages to display on each side of the current page. |
| Dots label | The placeholder between the inner and outer pages (leave blank to hide). 
Note: this label is translatable with the facetwp_i18n hook. |
| Prev button label | The “Prev” button label (leave blank to hide). 
Note: this label is translatable with the facetwp_i18n hook. The “Go to previous page” aria-label (present if a11y support is enabled) can be translated with __(), or with the gettext filter. |
| Next button label | The “Next” button label (leave blank to hide). 
Note: this label is translatable with the facetwp_i18n hook. The “Go to next page” aria-labels (present if a11y support is enabled) can be translated with __(), or with the gettext filter. |
| Scroll target | The target for scrolling the page when using the Pager facet. 
To target an element with a class, use a . before the class. For example, use .facetwp-template to scroll to the element with class="facetwp-template", which is the top of the listing/results.
To target an element with an id, use a # before the id. For example, use #myelement to scroll to th

the listing/results.
To target an element with an id, use a # before the id. For example, use #myelement to scroll to the element with id="myelement". 
To scroll to the top of the page, use body.
Leave the field blank for no scrolling. 
To customize the exact place where the page scroll needs to stop, use the Scroll offset setting. |
| Scroll offset | The number of px to modify the scroll target position. 
If you have entered a target in the Scroll target setting, you can modify the exact position where the scroll stops. 
Positive numbers are below the target, negative numbers above the target. For example, using 100 will make the scroll stop 100px below the target, and -100 will stop it 100px above the target. |

Note:When using the “Page numbers” pager type, the HTML output of the pager links (the numbers, dots, and “Prev”/”Next” links) can be modified with [the facetwp_facet_pager_link hook](/help-center/developers/hooks/output-hooks/facetwp_facet_pager_link/).

### “Result counts” pager type

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Count text (plural) | The text when there are multiple results. 
Available dynamic placeholders that you can use in the text for the different count types: 

[lower] – Lower result number.
Note: when a Load more Pager facet type exists on the page, this will always be 1.

[upper] – Upper result number
[page] – Page number
[per_page] – Number of posts per page
[total_pages] – Total number of pages
[total] – Total number of filtered results
[total_unfiltered] – Total number of unfiltered results

Usage examples:
[lower] - [upper] of [total] results
Page [page] of [total_pages]
Showing [total] of [total_unfiltered] results
Note: this text is translatable with the facetwp_i18n hook. |
| Count text (singular) | The text when there is one result. 
Usage example:
1 result
Notes:

This text is translatable with the facetwp_i18n hook.
Don’t use dynamic placeholders in this setting (like in the “Count text (plural)” setting, they will not work. |
| Count text (no results) | The text when there are no results. 
Usage example:
No results
Note: this text is translatable with the facetwp_i18n hook. |

### “Load more” pager type

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Load more text | The button text. 
Note: this text is translatable with the facetwp_i18n hook. |
| Loading text | The button loading text. 
Note: this text is translatable with the facetwp_i18n hook. |

### “Per page” pager type

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Default label | Set the default dropdown label, or leave blank. 
Note: this label is translatable with the facetwp_i18n hook. |
| Per page options | A comma-separated list of choices.
Optionally add a non-numeric choice, for example “Show all”, to be used to show all results.
Warning:Be very careful with offering your users a “Show all” option. When you have a large number of results, retrieving them all at the same time can be very detrimental to your server. Unless you have a limited number of posts, we do not recommend using this feature.
Note: this “Show all” label text (or the label you give it) is translatable with the facetwp_i18n hook. |

## FacetWP and infinite scroll

We often get the question if FacetWP supports infinite scroll, added by for example WooCommerce or [Elementor](/help-center/using-facetwp-with/elementor/) infinite scroll plugins.

FacetWP does **not** support infinite scroll, which is [intentional](https://hackernoon.com/stop-infinite-scrolling-on-your-website-now-ie6rg31eu).

This means that plugins that add any form of infinity load / infinite scroll **will not work** as expected.

The closest thing is the [“load more” pager type](#load-more-pager-type) of the Pager facet, which generates a “load more” button, working similar to infinite scroll.

heading_path: The load more button and URL vars
text:
## The load more button and URL vars

The [“load more” pager type](#load-more-pager-type) of the Pager facet does not update URL vars. This means that if a user clicks the Back button to go back to the listing, the position in the pagination and the previously loaded items are lost.

This behaviour is intentional. Let’s say there are 20 items per page and the user click the “load more” button 5 times, this results in 100 total results on the page. They click to go to a result, then click the Back button. When that Back button is clicked, FacetWP would have to load all 100 items at once, straining the server.

We recommend sticking with the “normal” numbers-based pager type (or use 
```
target="_blank"
```

 to open results) unless you absolutely need a “load more” button.

## Pagination and WooCommerce

FacetWP has [built-in support for WooCommerce pagination](/help-center/using-facetwp-with/woocommerce/#using-woocommerce-pagination), so generally there is no need to use a Pager facet on shop pages.

A good reason to keep WooCommerce pagination is that you can keep your theme’s styling, while if you replace it with a Pager facet, you have to style the pagination to match your theme. But still you might want to to replace it, for example if you want to use a [“Load more” Pager type](#load-more-pager-type).

Be aware that if you decide to keep WooCommerce pagination, you may need to apply [some fixes](/help-center/using-facetwp-with/woocommerce/#fix-woocommerce-pagination-and-result-counts) to get pagination and result counts working properly, depending on your template.

If you decide to replace WooCommerce pagination with a Pager facet, make sure to [read these pointers](/help-center/using-facetwp-with/woocommerce/#replace-woocommerce-pagination-with-a-pager-facet).

heading_path: Fix duplicate results when using a Pager facet
text:
## Fix duplicate results when using a Pager facet

If you are seeing duplicate posts in your listing while using a Pager/Load more facet, or a [Sort facet](/help-center/facets/facet-types/sort/), the cause is almost always the way the posts are ordered in the query, which is determined by the [orderby query argument](https://developer.wordpress.org/reference/classes/wp_query/#order-orderby-parameters).

If results are ordered by a value that is the same (or empty) for multiple posts, or by a [random value](/random-ordering-in-facetwp/), MySQL does not have a fallback and will often sort erratically. For example, ordering by 
```
menu_order
```

 can be problematic, because it defaults to 
```
0
```

 if it is not explicitly set for each post.

In [this tutorial](https://facetwp.com/how-to-prevent-duplicate-results/) you can read more about which scenarios can cause this to happen, and how to fix it quickly by [adding a secondary, fallback sort order to the listing query.](/how-to-prevent-duplicate-results/#add-a-fallback-sort-order)

## Display an “x results found for [keywords]” message

If you are using a [Search facet](/help-center/facets/facet-types/search/) on a page that also has a [Result counts](#result-counts-pager-type) Pager facet type, it is possible to extend the Pager facet’s text to display: “x results found for [keywords]”, when the Search facet is in use. See [this section on the Search facet page](/help-center/facets/facet-types/search/#display-an-x-results-found-for-keywords-message) for instructions.

## The Pager facet and SEO

If you are using a Pager facet for pagination on archive pages, be aware that the individual posts on the subsequent paged pages, and the paged pages themselves, will not be seen and indexed by search engines. The Pager facet’s 
```
<a>
```

 tags do not have 
```
href
```

 attributes with links that the search engine spider can follow. Also, users without JavaScript enabled will not be able to see and use any pagination on paged archives that you are using FacetWP on.

For SEO, this is not necessarily problematic, as long as all individual posts are reachable for the search engine spider through *other* archive pages on the site, like post-type archives and term archives. Another way to make sure all pages are found is by implementing a sitemap and [pointing to it in your robots.txt file](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/create-robots-txt).

If you are concerned about the implications for SEO or accessibility of using the Pager facet’s AJAX-based pagination, read [this section that lists a few possible approaches](/help-center/developers/the-facetwp-url/#facetwp-pagination-seo-and-accessibility).

heading_path: How to use a different post per page on the first page
text:
## How to use a different post per page on the first page

Sometimes we get the question of how to use a different number of posts per page on the first page of a [listing](/help-center/listing-templates/). A use case would be to show for example 10 posts when the page loads at first, and then, each time when clicking the [“Load more” Pager facet button](#load-more-pager-type), load 20 extra posts, until the query runs out of posts.

This is possible, but not trivial: WordPress calculates which posts to show on a page based on the current page number, the number of posts per page, the total number of pages, and the total number of posts.

[This tutorial](/how-to-use-a-different-post-per-page-on-the-first-page/) shows how to accomplish this, by letting WordPress recalculate the pagination parameters dynamically.

## What is the “Legacy” Proximity facet?

In **FacetWP v4.4 and newer**, you can choose between **two Proximity facet types**:

- The Legacy Proximity facet – uses Google’s legacy “**Places API**” – as described on this page.
- The [new Proximity facet](/help-center/facets/facet-types/proximity/) – uses Google’s “**Places API (New)**.

This split was introduced to let existing users decide when to migrate to the new Proximity facet. **Migrating to the new version is optional but recommended**.

To learn more about the context of the Proximity and [Map facet](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map-legacy/) changes in FacetWP v4.4, and why you should consider migrating to the new versions, read the [news article about the release](/introducing-the-new-proximity-and-map-facets-in-facetwp-v4-4/).

### The “Use Legacy Proximity facet” switch

![To use the Legacy Proximity facet, enable the 'Use Legacy Proximity facet' setting, enable the legacy 'Places API', and disable the 'Places API (New)' in the Google Cloud Console.](https://facetwp.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/use-legacy-proximity-facet.png)To use the Legacy Proximity facet, enable the “Use Legacy Proximity facet” setting, enable the legacy “Places API”, and disable “Places API (New)” in the Google Cloud Console.
The switch between the Legacy and new Proximity facet is determined by the new “Use Legacy Proximity facet” setting, which is located under 
```
FacetWP > Settings
```

.

This setting is only available in **FacetWP v4.4 and newer**, and is only visible if you have entered a key in the “Google Maps API key” setting above it.

To use (or keep using) the Legacy Proximity facet, **enable** this setting. If you do so, make sure the [Google’s legacy “Places API” is enabled](#enable-the-required-google-apis). To migrate to the new Proximity facet, follow the [migration instructions below](#how-to-migrate-to-the-new-proximity-facet).

grate to the new Proximity facet, follow the [migration instructions below](#how-to-migrate-to-the-new-proximity-facet).

Note that this switch between the Legacy and new Proximity facet is site-wide: you can’t set it differently for specific pages or Proximity facets. If needed, [the switch can also be set (or overridden) programmatically](#set-the-use-legacy-proximity-facet-switch-programmatically).

#### Existing users

If you already had a key entered in the “Google Maps API key” setting before you updated to FacetWP4.4+, the “Use Legacy Proximity facet” setting will be enabled by default and you are still using the Legacy Proximity facet. You can choose yourself if you want to migrate to the [new Proximity facet](/help-center/facets/facet-types/proximity/) and when. Make sure to [read the migration instructions](#how-to-migrate-to-the-new-proximity-facet).

-types/proximity/) and when. Make sure to [read the migration instructions](#how-to-migrate-to-the-new-proximity-facet).

To future-proof your site, we recommend migrating to the new version. But you can decide to keep using the Legacy Proximity facet for now. It will keep working until Google decides to discontinue the legacy “Places API” at an unknown point in the future. We recommend keeping an eye on Google’s [legacy](https://developers.google.com/maps/legacy) and [deprecations](https://developers.google.com/maps/deprecations) pages.

Note:The legacy “Places API” needed for the Legacy Proximity facet can no longer be enabled in Google Cloud Console after March 1, 2025. This means that existing API users can continue or choose to use the legacy “Places API” with the Legacy Proximity facet, but new API users have no choice but to use the new Proximity facet with the “Places API (New)”.

#### New users

#### New users

If you are a new FacetWP or Proximity facet user, or you did not already have an API key entered before updating FacetWP to v4.4+, the “Use Legacy Proximity facet” setting will be disabled by default. In this situation, there is no reason to use the Legacy Proximity facet. We recommend keeping the setting **disabled** and starting to use the [new Proximity facet](/help-center/facets/facet-types/proximity/) right away.

#### Users with FacetWP versions older than v4.4

For **FacetWP versions older than v4.4**, there is no choice and you will automatically be using the Legacy Proximity facet.

## How the Proximity facet works

![FacetWP Proximity facet - filter by distance to location](https://facetwp.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/facetwp-proximity-facet.gif)The Proximity facet lets you find results near a specified location, entered manually, or by clicking the [“Locate me” button](#the-locate-me-button).

After a user enters a location and clicks a place in the autocomplete dropdown, a radius can be chosen from [a pre-defined list](#radius-options), with a [dropdown or slider](#radius-ui). Results within that radius from the chosen location are then displayed in the listing, and (if available) on the [map](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map-legacy/).

Important:For “Locate me” to work, your site needs to be [HTTPS-enabled](https://developers.google.com/web/updates/2016/04/geolocation-on-secure-contexts-only).

heading_path: How location, place center points and radius work
text:
### How location, place center points and radius work

After clicking a place in the dropdown, FacetWP uses Google’s Places API to fetch the 
```
latitude, longitude
```

 of that places’s **central point**. Results within the user-defined radius of that point are displayed.

![Proximity facet radius and countries / regions](https://facetwp.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/proximity-radius-regions.jpg)A Proximity search for the region “Lombardy, Italy” (with the red border and blue marker at its geographical center). When the radius is set to 40km, it does **not** return any results in its capital Milan.
The facet does **not** understand geographic / political boundaries. If you search for a country (e.g. “Italy”), the facet will return results extending from that country’s **geographical center point** (as defined by the Google Places API (New)), which may include results from other countries if the chosen radius is large enough.

heading_path: How location, place center points and radius work
text:
ed by the Google Places API (New)), which may include results from other countries if the chosen radius is large enough.

Be aware that this behavior is possibly confusing for users. For example, if a user searches for the region Lombardy (Italy), they may expect to see results within the whole region (including its capital Milan). They may even expect results with a radius extending from the border of the region, not the center point. The Lombardy region is about 220km from west to east. So if a user searches it with a radius set to 40km, the facet will only display results within a circle of 80km diameter around Lombardy’s center point, which covers only a small part of the region, and does not include its capital Milan.

Keep this behavior in mind when choosing [radius options](#radius-options) for your situation. If you expect users to often search for regions or even countries, it makes sense to offer higher radius settings that cover whole regions or countries. Also, setting the [default radius](#default-radius) to a higher value can make the initial results more intuitively correct.

heading_path: How location, place center points and radius work
text:
, setting the [default radius](#default-radius) to a higher value can make the initial results more intuitively correct.

Another approach would be to [limit what “Place Types” are returned by the autocomplete results](#limit-autocomplete-results-to-specific-place-types), and exclude regions and countries. And/or to [limit results to a specific country or region](#limit-autocomplete-results-to-a-specific-country-or-region), or [bias/restrict autocomplete results towards a specific geographical area](#bias-or-restrict-autocomplete-results-towards-a-specific-area).

heading_path: Combine a Proximity facet with a Map facet
text:
### Combine a Proximity facet with a Map facet

If you use a Proximity facet on its own, it will return results within the chosen radius from the specified location. But there is no map for the user to interact with, nor any other feedback that includes distances.

You can [show the resulting posts’ distances to the specified location](#display-the-post-distance), and/or let users [sort results by distance](#sort-results-by-distance). But to give users visual feedback, a Proximity facet can very well be combined with a [Map facet](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map-legacy/).

When a location and radius are set (or changed) with the Proximity facet, the map will automatically zoom in or out, showing the locations that are within the radius of the set location.

heading_path: Combine a Proximity facet with a Map facet
text:

If the Proximity facet is in use, it will display a yellow marker pin at the set location. This marker pin can be [customized](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map-legacy/advanced-map-customizations-legacy/customize-marker-pins-legacy/#customize-the-proximity-facet-marker-pin), [disabled](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map-legacy/advanced-map-customizations-legacy/customize-marker-pins-legacy/#disable-the-proximity-facet-marker-pin), or [excluded from marker clustering behavior](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map-legacy/advanced-map-customizations-legacy/customize-marker-clustering-legacy/#exclude-the-proximity-marker-pin-from-marker-clustering)).

## How to get a Google Maps API key

For the Proximity (and [Map](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map-legacy/)) facets to work, you need to enter a valid Google Maps API key in the “Google Maps API key” setting in FacetWP’s settings. To [get](#1-create-a-google-maps-api-key-in-google-cloud-console), [set](#2-add-the-google-maps-api-key-to-facetwp) and [test](#3-test-google-api-connection) your API key, follow these steps:

heading_path: 1. Create a Google Maps API key in Google Cloud Console
text:
### 1. Create a Google Maps API key in Google Cloud Console

#### Set up Google Cloud Console and a project

To get a Google Maps API key, you need a [Google Cloud Console](https://cloud.google.com/) account. If you don’t have one, [set up a new account](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/cloud-setup/).

In your account, [create a project for your website, and set up billing](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/cloud-setup/).

#### Set up billing

To be able to use the API key you are going to create, you first need to [set up a Billing Account](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/manage-billing-account) in Google Cloud Console, and add your project to it. You will need a credit card to do so.

Your account will be billed for each request to the three above APIs. However, Google offers free credits, making usage free in practice for sites that are not heavily visited.

### Places/Autocomplete session tokens and billing

When using a Proximity facet, and typing in the input field, an “Autocomplete” request is done to the “Places/Autocomplete” API, which returns the predicted places in the Proximity facet’s dropdown. This request would normally be billed as one “Autocomplete” request. Next, when clicking one of the five predicted Places in the dropdown, a “Places Details” request is done, fetching its location. Normally this request would be billed separately.

FacetWP optimizes these costs by using a single [session token](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/place-autocomplete#session_tokens) for both the “Autocomplete” and the “Places Details” request. When re-using the same session token like this, Google groups both requests into a single session when billed.

As long as the user does not click a Place in the dropdown, the Autocomplete requests will be using the same token, also when searching for new Places. The session is only ended after a Place in the dropdown is clicked (also without new typing in the input field). A new session token is created again when the user starts typing in the field again.

out new typing in the input field). A new session token is created again when the user starts typing in the field again.

You can read more about session pricing [here](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/session-pricing). Check Google’s [pricing page](https://mapsplatform.google.com/pricing/) and the [Pricing Calculator](https://mapsplatform.google.com/pricing/#pricing-calculator) to estimate your potential costs.

## The “Locate me” button

When the user clicks the “Locate me” button, the Proximity facet tries to determine the user’s location and uses that as the center point for the search. The radius setting determines the size of the area around that center point.

Important:For “Locate me” to work, your site needs to be [HTTPS-enabled](https://developers.google.com/web/updates/2016/04/geolocation-on-secure-contexts-only).

### Accuracy of the “Locate me” button

When the “Locate me” button is clicked, FacetWP attempts to determine the user’s location. FacetWP first makes a browser [Geolocation API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Geolocation_API) request, which returns an **approximate** latitude/longitude based on the user’s IP address.

Then FacetWP performs a reverse lookup to determine the human-friendly physical address. This is **not an exact science**, and occasionally the location can be off by several kilometers.

## Customize Places autocomplete options

The Places API that the Legacy Proximity facet uses to predict and autocomplete Places while you type (and fetch its location when you click one), has several [customizable autocomplete options](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/reference/places-autocomplete-service#AutocompletionRequest). The most useful options are listed below.

### Localize the autocomplete predictions

There are two Places Autocomplete options involved when localizing the Proximity facet’s autocomplete predictions: [language](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/reference/places-autocomplete-service#AutocompletionRequest.language) and [region](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/reference/places-autocomplete-service#AutocompletionRequest.region). For best results, **use them both together**.

To set the language in which to show the Proximity facet’s autocomplete predictions, use the 
```
language
```

 option. If you don’t explicitly set a language, it will default to the browser’s language preference. The language code needs to be a [IETF BCP-47 language code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IETF_language_tag).

The 
```
region
```

 option affects address formatting and ranking of prediction results, and may influence what results are returned. This does **not** restrict results to the specified region.

This example returns results in German and sets the region to Germany:

*not** restrict results to the specified region.

This example returns results in German and sets the region to Germany:

```
How to use custom PHP code?PHP code can be added to your (child) theme's functions.php file. Alternatively, you can use the Custom Hooks add-on, or a code snippets plugin. More infoadd_filter( 'facetwp_proximity_autocomplete_options', function( $options ) {
  $options['language'] = 'de'; // Show predictions in German
  $options['region'] = 'de'; // Make formatting and ranking region-based.
  return $options;
});
```

Note that the 
```
region
```

 needs to be specified as a [ccTLD (“top-level domain”)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_code_top-level_domain#Latin_Character_ccTLDs) **two-character** value. Most ccTLD codes are identical to IETF BCP-47 language codes, with some notable exceptions. For example, the United Kingdom’s ccTLD is “uk” (.co.uk) while its language code is “en-GB”. To demonstrate this, the following example shows prediction results in British English language, and sets the region to the UK:

### Bias or restrict autocomplete results towards a specific area

With the [locationBias option](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/reference/places-autocomplete-service#AutocompletionRequest.locationBias), it is possible to bias the autocomplete prediction results towards a specific area by setting a location with 
```
lat/lng
```

 coordinates, and defining a “bounding box” surrounding that location.

The following example sets New York City as location and defines a bounding box with sides of approximately 10km away from the specified center.

The prediction results in the facet will now be **biased towards, but not restricted to** to places within the bounding box.

You can test this example code by entering “Amsterdam” in the Proximity facet’s field. The first prediction result will be a billiards club in New York with that name, and not the capital of the Netherlands, which would otherwise be the first.

### Limit autocomplete results to specific Place Types

With the [types](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/reference/places-autocomplete-service#AutocompletionRequest.types) option, it is possible to limit the autocomplete results to certain “Place Types”, like countries, regions, cities, municipalities or postal codes. A list of available Place Types can be found in the [Places API documentation](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/supported_types).

This code example limits the autocomplete results to 
```
(cities)
```

 only. See Table 3 in the documentation.

```
How to use custom PHP code?PHP code can be added to your (child) theme's functions.php file. Alternatively, you can use the Custom Hooks add-on, or a code snippets plugin. More info<?php
add_filter( 'facetwp_proximity_autocomplete_options', function( $options ) {
  $options['types'] = ['(cities)']; // The '(cities)' type is listed in Table 3. You can only use 1 item from Table 3.
  return $options;
});
```

heading_path: Fix issues with the number of autocomplete results
text:
### Fix issues with the number of autocomplete results

The Google Places API returns a maximum of 5 autocomplete results. Unfortunately, this number [cannot be changed](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/places/web-service/autocomplete#PlacesAutocompleteResponse).

This may lead to issues where some search terms (like zip codes) do not show up in the dropdown because there are more than 5 results for it. A solution can be to [limit autocomplete results to a specific country or region](#limit-autocomplete-results-to-a-specific-country-or-region), to [bias or restrict them towards a specific area](#bias-or-restrict-autocomplete-results-towards-a-specific-area), or to [limit them to specific place types, like region](#limit-autocomplete-results-to-specific-place-types). This will narrow the search, leading to a smaller number of autocomplete results.

Important:All info on this page refers to FacetWP’s “new” Proximity facet, which is available in **FacetWP v4.4 and newer**. To use or migrate to the new Proximity facet type (from the [Legacy Proximity facet](/help-center/facets/facet-types/proximity-legacy/)), read the [usage instructions below](#usage-instructions). Learn more about the context of the Proximity and Map facet changes in FacetWP v4.4 in the [news article about the release](/introducing-the-new-proximity-and-map-facets-in-facetwp-v4-4/).

## Usage instructions

In **FacetWP v4.4 and newer**, there are **two** Proximity facet types:

- The [Legacy Proximity facet](/help-center/facets/facet-types/proximity-legacy/) – uses Google’s legacy “**Places API**”.
- The new Proximity facet – uses Google’s “**Places API (New)**” – as described on this page.

This split was introduced to let existing users decide when to migrate to the new Proximity facet. **Migrating to the new version is optional but recommended**.

To learn more about the context of the Proximity and [Map facet](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map/) changes in FacetWP v4.4, and why you should consider migrating, read the [news article about the release](/introducing-the-new-proximity-and-map-facets-in-facetwp-v4-4/).

### The “Use Legacy Proximity facet” switch

![To use the new Proximity facet, disable the 'Use Legacy Proximity facet' setting, enable 'Places API (New)', and disable the legacy 'Places API' in the Google Cloud Console.](https://facetwp.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/dont-use-legacy-proximity-facet.png)To use the new Proximity facet, disable the “Use Legacy Proximity facet” setting, enable “Places API (New)”, and disable the legacy “Places API” in the Google Cloud Console.
The switch between the Legacy and new Proximity facet is determined by the new “Use Legacy Proximity facet” setting, which is located under 
```
FacetWP > Settings
```

.

This setting is only available in **FacetWP v4.4 and newer**, and is only visible if you have entered a key in the “Google Maps API key” setting above it.

To use the new Proximity facet, **disable** this setting. If you do so, make sure [Google’s Places API (New) is enabled](#enable-the-required-google-apis). Make sure to [read the migration instructions](/help-center/facets/facet-types/proximity-legacy/#how-to-migrate-to-the-new-proximity-facet) if you already had a Proximity facet before updating to FacetWP4.4+.

-legacy/#how-to-migrate-to-the-new-proximity-facet) if you already had a Proximity facet before updating to FacetWP4.4+.

Note that this switch between the Legacy and new Proximity facet is site-wide: you can’t set it differently for specific pages or Proximity facets. If needed, [the switch can also be set (or overridden) programmatically](#set-the-use-legacy-proximity-facet-switch-programmatically).

#### Existing users

If you already had a key entered in the “Google Maps API key” setting before you updated to FacetWP4.4+, the “Use Legacy Proximity facet” setting will be enabled by default and you are still using the [Legacy Proximity facet](/help-center/facets/facet-types/proximity-legacy/). You can choose yourself if you want to migrate to the new Proximity facet and when. Make sure to [read the migration instructions](/help-center/facets/facet-types/proximity-legacy/#how-to-migrate-to-the-new-proximity-facet).

he migration instructions](/help-center/facets/facet-types/proximity-legacy/#how-to-migrate-to-the-new-proximity-facet).

To future-proof your site, we recommend migrating to the new version. But you can decide to keep using the Legacy Proximity facet for now. It will keep working until Google decides to discontinue the legacy “Places API” at an unknown point in the future. We recommend keeping an eye on Google’s [legacy](https://developers.google.com/maps/legacy) and [deprecations](https://developers.google.com/maps/deprecations) pages.

Note:The legacy “Places API” needed for the Legacy Proximity facet can no longer be enabled in Google Cloud Console after March 1, 2025. This means that existing API users can continue or choose to use the legacy “Places API” with the Legacy Proximity facet, but new API users have no choice but to use the new Proximity facet with the “Places API (New)”.

#### New users

If you are a new FacetWP or Proximity facet user, or you did not already have an API key entered before updating FacetWP to v4.4+, the “Use Legacy Proximity facet” setting will be disabled by default. In this situation, there is no reason to use the Legacy Proximity facet. We recommend keeping the setting disabled and start using the new Proximity facet:

1. Go to 
```
FacetWP > Settings
```

 and make sure the “Use Legacy Proximity facet” setting is **disabled**. Note that this setting is only visible if you have entered a key in the “Google Maps API key” setting above it.
2. In your Google Cloud Console, [enable “Places API (New)”, and disable the legacy “Places API”](#enable-the-required-google-apis), both also in your [key restrictions](#restrict-your-api-key). (If you do not already have a Google Cloud Console account, and an API key, [see the Google Maps API key section below](#how-to-get-a-google-maps-api-key)).

#### Users with FacetWP versions older than v4.4

#### Users with FacetWP versions older than v4.4

For FacetWP versions older than v4.4, there is no choice and you will automatically be using the [Legacy Proximity facet](/help-center/facets/facet-types/proximity-legacy/).

## How the Proximity facet works

![FacetWP Proximity facet - filter by distance to location](https://facetwp.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/facetwp-proximity-facet.gif)The Proximity facet lets you find results near a specified location, entered manually, or by clicking the [“Locate me” button](#the-locate-me-button).

After a user enters a location and clicks a place in the autocomplete dropdown, a radius can be chosen from [a pre-defined list](#radius-options), with a [dropdown or slider](#radius-ui). Results within that radius from the chosen location are then displayed in the listing, and (if available) on the [map](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map/).

Important:For “Locate me” to work, your site needs to be [HTTPS-enabled](https://developers.google.com/web/updates/2016/04/geolocation-on-secure-contexts-only).

heading_path: How location, place center points and radius work
text:
### How location, place center points and radius work

After clicking a place in the dropdown, FacetWP uses Google’s Places API (New) to fetch the 
```
latitude, longitude
```

 of that places’s **central point**. Results within the user-defined radius of that point are displayed.

![Proximity facet radius and countries / regions](https://facetwp.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/proximity-radius-regions.jpg)A Proximity search for the region “Lombardy, Italy” (with the red border and blue marker at its geographical center). When the radius is set to 40km, it does **not** return any results in its capital Milan.
The facet does **not** understand geographic / political boundaries. If you search for a country (e.g. “Italy”), the facet will return results extending from that country’s **geographical center point** (as defined by the Google Places API (New)), which may include results from other countries if the chosen radius is large enough.

heading_path: How location, place center points and radius work
text:
ed by the Google Places API (New)), which may include results from other countries if the chosen radius is large enough.

Be aware that this behavior is possibly confusing for users. For example, if a user searches for the region Lombardy (Italy), they may expect to see results within the whole region (including its capital Milan). They may even expect results with a radius extending from the border of the region, not the center point. The Lombardy region is about 220km from west to east. So if a user searches it with a radius set to 40km, the facet will only display results within a circle of 80km diameter around Lombardy’s center point, which covers only a small part of the region, and does not include its capital Milan.

Keep this behavior in mind when choosing [radius options](#radius-options) for your situation. If you expect users to often search for regions or even countries, it makes sense to offer higher radius settings that cover whole regions or countries. Also, setting the [default radius](#default-radius) to a higher value can make the initial results more intuitively correct.

heading_path: Combine a Proximity facet with a Map facet
text:
### Combine a Proximity facet with a Map facet

If you use a Proximity facet on its own, it will return results within the chosen radius from the specified location. But there is no map for the user to interact with, nor any other feedback that includes distances.

You can [show the resulting posts’ distances to the specified location](#display-the-post-distance), and/or let users [sort results by distance](#sort-results-by-distance). But to give users visual feedback, a Proximity facet can very well be combined with a [Map facet](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map/).

When a location and radius are set (or changed) with the Proximity facet, the map will automatically zoom in or out, showing the locations that are within the radius of the set location.

## How to get a Google Maps API key

For the Proximity (and [Map](/help-center/facets/facet-types/map/)) facets to work, you need to enter a valid Google Maps API key in the “Google Maps API key” setting in FacetWP’s settings. To [get](#1-create-a-google-maps-api-key-in-google-cloud-console), [set](#2-add-the-google-maps-api-key-to-facetwp) and [test](#3-test-google-api-connection) your API key, follow these steps:

heading_path: 1. Create a Google Maps API key in Google Cloud Console
text:
### 1. Create a Google Maps API key in Google Cloud Console

#### Set up Google Cloud Console and a project

To get a Google Maps API key, you need a [Google Cloud Console](https://cloud.google.com/) account. If you don’t have one, [set up a new account](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/cloud-setup/).

In your account, [create a project for your website, and set up billing](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/cloud-setup/).

#### Set up billing

To be able to use the API key you are going to create, you first need to [set up a Billing Account](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/manage-billing-account) in Google Cloud Console, and add your project to it. You will need a credit card to do so.

Your account will be billed for each request to the three above APIs. However, Google offers free credits, making usage free in practice for sites that are not heavily visited.

Before March 1, 2025, Google offered a free monthly credit of $200. On March 1, 2025, [this has changed](https://mapsplatform.google.com/resources/blog/build-more-for-free-and-access-more-discounts-online-with-google-maps-platform-updates/) to a free monthly usage threshold of 10K requests for each product. Check the [pricing page](https://mapsplatform.google.com/pricing/) and the [Pricing Calculator](https://mapsplatform.google.com/pricing/#pricing-calculator) to estimate your costs.

Note that FacetWP [optimizes billing costs for using the Places API (New), by using session tokens](#places-autocomplete-session-tokens-and-billing).

#### Enable the required Google APIs

In your project, enable the following three APIs under 
```
APIs & Services > Enable APIs and services
```

1. **Maps JavaScript API**: required for the Map / Proximity facets to work.
2. **Geocoding API**: required for the Proximity facet’s “Locate me” button.
3. **Places API (New)**: required for the Proximity facet’s autocomplete function.

In FacetWP version 4.4+, you can test the correct connection to the [above three Google APIs](#enable-the-required-google-apis).

To run the test, go to

```

Note that if the “Use Legacy Proximity facet” setting is enabled, you’ll see an extra button to test the legacy “Places API”, which is needed for the [Legacy Proximity facet](/help-center/facets/facet-types/proximity-legacy/). In this case, the “Places API (New)” test is irrelevant.

If any of the required three test results is red and says “connection failed”, check all [API key settings and restrictions in your Google Cloud project](#how-to-get-a-google-maps-api-key). Make sure the three needed APIs are enabled, and available in your project.

**It may take up to 5 minutes for changed Google Cloud Console settings to take effect**.

Note that the Geocoding API needs the Maps JavaScript API enabled and correctly connected. If the Geocoding API test keeps failing, reload the page and/or clear your browser cache and try again.

To get more information about a failed connection, you can also check the front-end page that contains the Map/Proximity facet(s). Make sure to clear your browser cache first. Then open the browser console, reload the page and check for errors happening before, during or after using the facet(s). If you see any errors, you can [look up the meaning of the error message](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/error-messages).

Note:If you [add your API key to FacetWP programmatically](#add-the-api-key-programmatically) (and the key field is empty), the API test feature is not available. In this situation, you can temporarily remove the hook and manually enter your key in the setting to test the APIs.

### Places/Autocomplete session tokens and billing

When using a Proximity facet, and typing in the input field, an “Autocomplete” request is done to the “Places/Autocomplete (New)” API, which returns the predicted places in the Proximity facet’s dropdown. This request would normally be billed as one “Autocomplete” request. Next, when clicking one of the five predicted Places in the dropdown, a “Places Details” request is done, fetching its location. Normally this request would be billed separately.

FacetWP optimizes these costs by using a single [session token](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/place-autocomplete#session_tokens) for both the “Autocomplete” and the “Places Details” request. When re-using the same session token like this, Google groups both requests into a single session when billed.

As long as the user does not click a Place in the dropdown, the Autocomplete requests will be using the same token, also when searching for new Places. The session is only ended after a Place in the dropdown is clicked (also without new typing in the input field). A new session token is created again when the user starts typing in the field again.

out new typing in the input field). A new session token is created again when the user starts typing in the field again.

You can read more about session pricing [here](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/session-pricing). Check Google’s [pricing page](https://mapsplatform.google.com/pricing/) and the [Pricing Calculator](https://mapsplatform.google.com/pricing/#pricing-calculator) to estimate your potential costs.

## The “Locate me” button

When the user clicks the “Locate me” button, the Proximity facet tries to determine the user’s location and uses that as the center point for the search. The radius setting determines the size of the area around that center point.

Important:For “Locate me” to work, your site needs to be [HTTPS-enabled](https://developers.google.com/web/updates/2016/04/geolocation-on-secure-contexts-only).

### Accuracy of the “Locate me” button

When the “Locate me” button is clicked, FacetWP attempts to determine the user’s location. FacetWP first makes a browser [Geolocation API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Geolocation_API) request, which returns an **approximate** latitude/longitude based on the user’s IP address.

Then FacetWP performs a reverse lookup to determine the human-friendly physical address. This is **not an exact science**, and occasionally the location can be off by several kilometers.
